title: The Cherokee Nation before removal
description: By the 1820s the Cherokee had Sequoyah’s syllabary (1821), a written constitution (1827) and the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper (1828).

facts.text: By 1821 Sequoyah had created a Cherokee writing system of 86 symbols, one for each syllable, and literacy spread quickly.
The Cherokee Nation adopted a written constitution in 1827 and began printing the Cherokee Phoenix, a Native nation's first newspaper, in 1828.

title: Worcester v. Georgia
description: The Indian Removal Act (1830) pressed Southeastern nations west; in 1832 the Supreme Court ruled Georgia law had no force in the Cherokee Nation, but Georgia ignored it and Jackson declined to enforce it.

facts.text: In 1830 Congress passed the Indian Removal Act, pressing Native nations of the Southeast to give up their lands for territory west of the Mississippi.
In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that the Cherokee Nation was a distinct community where Georgia's laws had no force.
Georgia ignored the Worcester ruling, and President Andrew Jackson declined to enforce it.

title: The Trail of Tears
description: A small faction signed the Treaty of New Echota (1835); in 1838 the army forced more than 16,000 Cherokee west, and over 4,000 died by one estimate. Other Southeastern nations were removed too.

facts.text: In late 1835 a small faction signed the Treaty of New Echota, giving up Cherokee land in the East; none were elected Cherokee officials, most Cherokee opposed it, and the Senate ratified it in 1836.
In 1838 US soldiers and state militia forced more than 16,000 Cherokee from their homes into camps and then west to Indian Territory, today's Oklahoma.
Elizur Butler, a missionary doctor who traveled with the Cherokee, estimated that over 4,000 died, nearly a fifth of the nation.
The Choctaw, Muscogee Creek, Seminole and Chickasaw were also relocated to Indian Territory in the 1830s.
After removal the Cherokee rebuilt their nation in Indian Territory, and the Cherokee Nation remains an independent tribe.

title: The Erie Canal
description: Finished in 1825, the canal linked the Great Lakes to New York City, opening the interior and making the city the leading commercial center.

facts.text: The Erie Canal, finished in 1825, linked the Great Lakes to New York City by way of the Hudson River at Albany.
The Erie Canal opened the interior of the continent to settlement and made New York City the nation's leading commercial center.

title: The Lowell mill girls
description: Young women from New England farms worked 12 to 14 hour days in Lowell’s mills for cash wages and struck in the turnouts of 1834 and 1836.

facts.text: Lowell's textile corporations recruited young women, generally 15 to 30, from New England farms with few other chances, offering monthly cash wages and board.
Most Lowell mill workers labored 12 to 14 hours a day and lived in company boardinghouses with curfews.
In 1834 and 1836 Lowell's women workers went on strike in turnouts against a wage cut and higher board charges.

title: Irish and German newcomers
description: The Great Famine (from 1845) sent Irish emigrants to Northeastern cities; Irish and German Catholics met nativist opposition, including the Know-Nothing party of the 1850s.

facts.text: Potato blight struck Ireland in 1845; about one million people died in the Great Famine, and perhaps 2 million more emigrated.
Most Irish immigrants settled in the cities where they landed, almost all in the Northeast.
All of the Irish and many German immigrants were Roman Catholic, which fed anti-Catholic opposition to them.
The anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic Know-Nothing party flourished in the 1850s; members were told to say they knew nothing about it.
The Know-Nothings wanted immigrants to wait far longer, 21 years, before they could become citizens.

title: The cotton gin
description: Whitney’s 1793 gin cleaned sticky-seeded inland cotton, making it profitable to grow across the South.

facts.text: Long-staple cotton, whose seeds come out easily, grew only near the coast; the cotton that grew inland had sticky seeds that were slow to pick out.
Eli Whitney's cotton gin (1793) pulled cotton fiber through wire teeth on a turning cylinder, leaving the seeds behind.

title: How cotton spread slavery
description: The gin did not cut the labor of planting and picking, so profitable cotton raised demand for land and enslaved people.

facts.text: The gin did not reduce the need for enslaved people to plant and pick cotton; cotton became so profitable that demand for land and enslaved labor grew.

title: The domestic slave trade
description: After the 1808 ban on imports from Africa, up to a million enslaved people were forced from the Upper South to the Deep South, splitting families.

facts.text: Congress banned the importation of enslaved people from Africa in 1808.
The domestic slave trade forced up to a million enslaved people from the Upper South to cotton plantations in the Deep South.
Enslaved people sold south were often marched in chained gangs, and sales separated spouses and families.

title: Family under slavery
description: The law did not recognize enslaved marriages and sales split families, but communities honored marriages, for example by jumping the broom.

facts.text: Southern laws refused to recognize marriages between enslaved people, and enslavers often separated spouses by sale.
Enslaved communities took marriage seriously; some couples jumped the broom, a ritual that validated marriages the law would not.

title: Faith in the hush harbors
description: Against obedience preaching, enslaved believers worshiped in secret hush harbors, blending African rhythms and beliefs with evangelical Christianity.

facts.text: Preachers approved by enslavers often taught that obedience to one's master was the highest religious duty.
Using signals and passwords whites could not read, enslaved believers called one another to secret worship in the woods, called hush harbors.
In their own worship, enslaved people mixed African rhythms, singing and beliefs with evangelical Christianity.

title: Spirituals
description: Religious folksongs made by enslaved people, passed on by ear in call and response, often with a double meaning of salvation and freedom.

facts.text: Spirituals were religious folksongs created by enslaved people in the South, passed on only by ear and sung in call and response.
Many spirituals carried double meanings: religious salvation, and freedom from slavery.

title: Everyday resistance and Nat Turner’s revolt
description: Enslaved people resisted by slowing work, feigning illness and breaking tools; Nat Turner’s 1831 revolt was followed by killings and harsher laws.

facts.text: Some enslaved people resisted every day by slowing down work, pretending to be sick or breaking tools.
In August 1831 in Southampton County, Virginia, Nat Turner led a revolt in which at least 55 white people were killed.
After Turner's revolt, whites killed at least 100 Black people, many uninvolved, and Turner was hanged.
Turner's revolt set off new laws banning the education, movement and assembly of enslaved people.

title: The Underground Railroad
description: Freedom seekers often escaped on their own; a secret network of stations and conductors grew to help them reach the North, Canada, Mexico and beyond.

facts.text: Many freedom seekers escaped on their own, without help; over time, helpers of all races built a secret network to assist them.
The Underground Railroad borrowed railway words: safe houses were stations and guides were conductors.
Freedom seekers headed not only north but to Canada, Mexico, Spanish Florida and beyond.

title: Harriet Tubman
description: Tubman escaped in 1849 and made about 13 trips back to Maryland, never losing a passenger; older, larger counts are a legend.

facts.text: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 when she was about to be sold.
Tubman made about 13 trips back into Maryland to rescue family and friends, and later said she never lost a passenger.
An 1868 biography inflated Tubman's rescues to about 19 trips and 300 people; historians now accept about 13 trips.

title: Garrison and The Liberator
description: Garrison’s Liberator (1831) demanded immediate emancipation, and in 1833 he helped found the American Anti-Slavery Society.

facts.text: William Lloyd Garrison published the first issue of The Liberator on January 1, 1831, demanding immediate emancipation.
The first issue of The Liberator promised, in capital letters: "I WILL BE HEARD."
In 1833 Garrison helped organize the American Anti-Slavery Society.

title: Frederick Douglass, abolitionist
description: Douglass escaped in 1838, published his Narrative in 1845 to answer doubters, and started The North Star in 1847.

facts.text: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in September 1838 disguised as a sailor.
In 1845 Douglass published his Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, partly to answer those who doubted he had ever been enslaved.
In 1847 Douglass launched his own newspaper, The North Star, despite objections from Garrison and others.

title: Northern opposition to abolitionists
description: Many Northerners saw abolitionists as a threat to sectional harmony and the Constitution’s bargain; mobs killed Elijah Lovejoy in 1837.

facts.text: Many Northerners distrusted abolitionists, fearing they threatened harmony between North and South; immediate emancipation was unpopular even among many antislavery Northerners.
Abolitionists' critics argued that the Constitution left slavery to each state to decide.
Mobs destroyed Elijah Lovejoy's antislavery press several times, and on November 7, 1837, a mob in Alton, Illinois, killed him as he defended it.

title: Seneca Falls and its roots
description: Barred from the 1840 London antislavery convention, Mott and Stanton organized the 1848 Seneca Falls convention.

facts.text: At the 1840 World Anti-Slavery Convention in London, women delegates were refused seats; Lucretia Mott and Elizabeth Cady Stanton then agreed to hold a women's rights convention.
The first women's rights convention met at Seneca Falls, New York, on July 19 and 20, 1848.

title: The Declaration of Sentiments
description: Modeled on the Declaration of Independence (“all men and women are created equal”), it listed women’s legal grievances; its demand for the vote alone was not unanimous.

facts.text: Stanton's Declaration of Sentiments was modeled on the Declaration of Independence: "all men and women are created equal."
The Declaration of Sentiments said a married woman was, in the eye of the law, "civilly dead," with no right even to the wages she earned.
The resolution demanding women's right to the elective franchise, the vote, was the only one that did not pass unanimously.
Frederick Douglass spoke at Seneca Falls in support of women's rights.
In all, 100 people signed the Declaration of Sentiments: 68 women and 32 men.

title: Manifest Destiny
description: O’Sullivan’s 1845 phrase for the belief that the US had a God-given right to spread across the continent; Whigs called it arrogant.

facts.text: In 1845 the editor John L. O'Sullivan wrote of "our manifest destiny to overspread and to possess the whole of the continent."
Believers held that expanding to the Pacific was the nation's God-given right; Whigs attacked the idea as warlike and arrogant.

title: Texas, Oregon and the Mexican War
description: Texas joined in 1845 with a disputed border; Oregon was divided in 1846; war with Mexico (1846 to 1848) ended with Mexico ceding about 55 percent of its territory, while critics like Lincoln questioned the war.

facts.text: Texas won independence from Mexico in 1836 and joined the United States on December 29, 1845, but Mexico disputed its border: the Rio Grande or the Nueces River.
As settlers came on the Oregon Trail, an 1846 treaty with Britain divided the Oregon Country along the 49th parallel.
President James K. Polk sent troops into the disputed land, and after clashes there Congress declared war on Mexico on May 13, 1846.
In December 1847 Congressman Abraham Lincoln challenged Polk to show whether the spot where the war's first blood was shed was really US soil.
The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) ended the war; Mexico ceded about 55 percent of its territory, including California, for $15 million.

title: Mexicans in the ceded lands
description: The treaty promised Mexicans their property, but an 1851 law forced California landowners into costly title fights that often cost them the land.

facts.text: The treaty let Mexicans in the ceded lands stay and keep their property.
An 1851 law made Mexican landowners in California prove their titles, a slow, costly process; the cost was often the land itself.

title: The Missouri Compromise
description: In 1820 Missouri entered slave and Maine free, and slavery was barred north of 36°30′ in the Louisiana Territory.

facts.text: The Missouri Compromise (1820) admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, keeping the balance between them.
The Missouri Compromise banned slavery north of 36°30′ in the rest of the Louisiana Territory.

title: The Compromise of 1850
description: California entered free and New Mexico and Utah could decide, but the stricter Fugitive Slave Act turned many Northerners against slavery’s spread.

facts.text: The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a free state, let New Mexico and Utah territories decide on slavery, and ended the slave trade in Washington, DC.
Senator Henry Clay proposed the 1850 package, and Senator Stephen A. Douglas steered it through Congress.
The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850 required officials even in free states to arrest suspected freedom seekers and punished anyone who helped them escape.
The Fugitive Slave Act angered many in the North, turning moderate antislavery Northerners into firm opponents of slavery's spread.

title: The Kansas-Nebraska Act
description: In 1854 popular sovereignty replaced the Missouri line, and the rush of rival settlers produced Bleeding Kansas.

facts.text: The Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854), sponsored by Douglas, let settlers decide slavery by popular sovereignty, repealing the Missouri Compromise line.
Proslavery and antislavery settlers rushed into Kansas, and the violence earned it the name Bleeding Kansas.

title: A house divided
description: In 1858 Lincoln argued the nation could not endure permanently half slave and half free, summing up how cotton, expansion and failed compromises split the country.

facts.text: On June 16, 1858, in Springfield, Illinois, Abraham Lincoln said: "A house divided against itself cannot stand."
Lincoln added: "I believe this government cannot endure, permanently half slave and half free."
